April 4, 2026 | New Delhi: The Editors Guild of India is deeply concerned by both the contents and the underlying intent behind the Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (“Draft Amendments”), which were made public by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on March 30, 2026, with just a fortnight given for comments.
Prima facie, the amended rules and guidelines, whose stated purpose is to “strengthen compliance” and increase the effectiveness of regulatory oversight of content regulation mechanisms under Part III (Code of Ethics relating to Digital Media) of the IT Rules, 2021” appear to arm MeitY with sweeping powers of content regulation, sharply increases the compliance burden on digital intermediaries, and gives the executive overarching powers to block or take down content generated by  “non news publishers” and intermediaries. This will directly infringe the fundamental right to free speech guaranteed to all citizens under the Constitution and will have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the airing of contrarian views, which are fundamental to an open and functional democracy.
Sub-rule (4) to Rule 3, which deals with due diligence obligations of intermediaries, now makes it mandatory on the part of intermediaries to comply with “any clarification, advisory, order, direction, standard operating procedure, code of practice or guideline issued by the ministry, by order in writing”. Failure to comply has been linked to loss of the safe harbour protection extended to intermediaries and platforms for user-generated content, under section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The absence of due process for the issuance of compliance orders and the complete lack of transparency in the process are deeply concerning.
Changes to Rule 14(2) and Rule 14(5) in the draft amendment also greatly widen the powers of the Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC). IDC, a central oversight body constituted under Rule 14 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, was specifically created to hear grievances and complaints against digital content. Now, the IDC has been empowered to deal with and “matter” – a generalisation which arms the body to consider virtually any issue, in the absence of any definition of what constitutes a “matter”. Other provisions devolve rulemaking powers entirely to the executive branch, removing the window for legislative oversight provided under the IT Act.
The EGi calls on the government to urgently review or recall the draft rules, and engage in more constructive consultations with all sections of stakeholders and take on board valid concerns and objections.
Warm regards,
Sanjay Kapoor, President
Raghavan Srinivasan, General Secretary
Teresa Rehman, Treasurer

"Digital India" can process billions of UPI transactions, authenticate Aadhaar in seconds, deploy facial recognition, and run databases at population scale.

But ask the MEA a basic question: how many passports have been issued to non-citizens?

The reply: "We do not maintain consolidated data."

That answer raises a bigger question than the number itself.

Passport issuance today is a digital workflow. Applications generate electronic records. Identity and supporting documents are captured. 

Decisions are recorded. Passports are issued against individual files. 

In any properly designed database, producing an aggregate from structured records is exactly what a simple query is meant to do.

So, what does "we do not maintain consolidated data" actually mean?

Does the underlying information not exist in structured form?

Is it fragmented across systems that cannot be queried together?

Is citizenship or nationality not stored in a reliably searchable field?

Or does the government have the data but simply not compile or retrieve the aggregate?

These are very different explanations, and the public deserves a clear answer.

This matters because passports are not a minor administrative detail. 

The Passports Act explicitly deals with nationality and non-citizenship. 

If the State cannot readily determine, from its own passport system, how many documents fall into a legally significant category, that is a serious issue of data design, auditability, and institutional accountability.

And if the information can be generated from existing digital records but is still not being produced, then a harder question follows:

Is this a technical limitation, or a decision not to look?

Before celebrating "Digital India", we should ask something more basic:

Can the government interrogate its own databases when the public asks a legitimate question?

Because digitization without retrievability is just electronic filing.

And databases without accountability are not Digital India. They are digital opacity.

Pope Leo meets Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, pledging to keep working past differences
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV prayed Monday in the Vatican with the Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, and vowed to keep working to overcome differences in a historic meeting with the first female leader of the Church of England and the s
Nicole Winfield, The Associated Press
Apr 27, 2026 3:43 AM

VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV prayed Monday in the Vatican with the Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, and vowed to keep working to overcome differences in a historic meeting with the first female leader of the Church of England and the spiritual leader of the global Anglican Communion.

The encounter between Christianity’s two most famous religious figures would have been unthinkable just a few years ago, given the divisions between their two churches over women’s ordination and Mullally's appointment.

Leo acknowledged that “new problems” in their relationship had been added onto “historically divisive issues.” But he nevertheless vowed to continue the tradition of past popes to continue to try to reunite the churches.

Anglicans split from Rome in 1534, when English King Henry VIII was refused a marriage annulment. Despite a formal theological dialogue that began in the 1960s, big differences remain, especially over the Church of England’s decision to ordain women. The Roman Catholic Church reserves the priesthood for men.

Leo quoted Pope Francis as telling Anglican primates that “it would be a scandal if, due to our divisions, we did not fulfil our common vocation to make Christ known.”

“For my part, I add that it would also be a scandal if we did not continue to work towards overcoming our differences, no matter how intractable they may appear,” Leo said.

Mullally thanked Leo for welcoming her on her first foreign visit since she was installed last month.

Mullally, whose appointment has split the already divided Anglican Communion, arrived early to meet with Leo in his library. The two then prayed together in the Urban VIII Chapel inside the Apostolic palace for what the Vatican said was a “moment of prayer.” Mullally’s office said Leo presided but that they both “said the grace together.”

In her remarks to Leo, Mullally said both of them were called to preach the Gospel with “renewed clarity.”

“In the face of inhuman violence, deep division, and rapid societal change, we must keep telling a more hopeful story: that every human life has infinite value because we are precious children of God; that the human family is called to live as sisters and brothers,” she said. “We must therefore work together for the common good — always building bridges, never walls; that the poorest among us are closest to the heart of God.”

A pilgrimage to Rome amid challenges

Mullally is on what she has called a four-day pilgrimage to Rome that has included visits to the main pontifical basilicas, where she has prayed at the tombs of Saints Peter and Paul and met with top Vatican officials.

Lambeth Palace says her visit is designed “to strengthen Anglican–Roman Catholic relations through prayer, personal encounter, and formal theological dialogue. It aims to deepen bonds of communion, affirm a shared witness, and encourage ongoing collaboration at both global and local levels.”

The first female Anglican priests were ordained in 1994, its first female bishop in 2015, and now Mullally as the first archbishop of Canterbury.

Leo and Mullally have already exchanged greetings, with Leo congratulating her on her installation last month but acknowledging she was taking over at a “challenging” time and that differences still divide the Anglican and Catholic churches.

“We also know that the ecumenical journey has not always been smooth,” Leo wrote. “Despite much progress, our immediate predecessors, Pope Francis and Archbishop Justin Welby, acknowledged frankly that new circumstances have presented new disagreements among us,” Leo wrote.

He nevertheless vowed to continue dialogue, and in October Leo welcomed King Charles III and Queen Camilla to the Vatican, where they prayed in the Sistine Chapel. Charles is the titular head of the Church of England.

That event, Oct. 25, marked the first time since the Reformation that the heads of the two Christian churches had prayed together.

This year marks the 60th anniversary of the first formal ecumenical statement between the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches, signed in 1966 at St. Paul’s Outside the Walls basilica by Archbishop Michael Ramsey and Pope Paul VI.

Mullally for her part has expressed solidarity with Leo’s peace message, after the American-born pope was harshly criticized by President Donald Trump for his calls for peace in Iran.

Popes past have met with female Christian bishops and archbishops: Francis met in 2015 with Archbishop Antje Jackelén, the first woman to lead the Lutheran Church of Sweden. Francis also invited the female Anglican bishop, Jo Bailey Wells, into a private meeting of his cardinal advisers in 2024 to discuss the role of women in the Catholic Church.

An historic meeting that follows the king's visit

George Gross, an expert on theology and the monarchy at King’s College London, said the meeting was historic, particularly given the Vatican doesn't recognize the female priesthood.

“If we were to go back several hundred years, it’s unthinkable,” he said. “It’s the fact that the pope is willing to meet, but in itself it also shows the difference, the gap.”

Gross said the prayer was clearly an attempt to show the two churches united, especially in confronting the global conflicts and projecting a message of unity. Such optics, he said, were in continuity with the visit to the Vatican in October by the king.

“It’s a doubling down of togetherness,” he said.

An appointment that divides the Anglican communion

Her appointment though has split the Anglican Communion, whose 100 million members in 165 countries are deeply divided over issues such as the role of women and the treatment of LGBTQ+ people. Many in England and other Western countries hailed her appointment as a historic breaking of a stained-glass ceiling.

But the communion’s largest and fastest-growing churches in Africa belong to a conservative group called the Global Anglican Future Conference, or Gafcon, which has sharply criticized her appointment and threatened a final break. In the U.S., the conservative Anglican Church in North America formed in a break from the more liberal U.S. and Canadian Episcopal churches and has signed onto the Gafcon statement opposing Mullally’s appointment.

In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.

A bridge between East and West

In his reflection, the cardinal begins immediately by addressing the devastation caused by the conflicts that are ravaging the Middle East and which have their roots in a lack of understanding and the difficulties of dialogue between East and West. "The world is divided. The West," he observes, "is based on economic interests, secularism, pragmatism and weapons, and struggles to understand the logic of an East that is profoundly different, where religion becomes not only a doctrine but also an ideology" that shapes every aspect of life. Cardinal Sako was born in Zākhō (northern Iraq) on 4 July 1949. He completed his primary education in Mosul, before attending the local St Jean seminary, run by the French Dominican Fathers. Ordained a priest on 1 May 1974, he carried out pastoral work at Mosul Cathedral until 1979. Sent to Rome, he studied at the Pontifical Oriental Institute, obtaining a doctorate in Oriental Patrology, followed by a doctorate in History at the Sorbonne in Paris and a licentiate in Islamic Studies.

From 1997 to 2002, he served as rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. Upon his return to Mosul, he took charge of the Parish of Perpetual Help until his election as Archbishop of Kirkuk on 27 September 2003, with his episcopal ordination taking place on 14 November. On 31 January 2013, at the synod convened in Rome by Pope Benedict XVI following the resignation of Patriarch Cardinal Emmanuel Delly, he was elected Primate and received the Ecclesiastica Communio from the Pope on 1 February. On 28 June 2018, Pope Francis created him a cardinal. He is a member of the Dicastery for the Oriental Churches, for Culture and Education, for Interreligious Dialogue, and of the Council for the Economy.

When discussing Iran, it is essential to understand that "we are not merely dealing with a political phenomenon; we must also take the religious dimension into account. 🚨 Digital State + New Laws in Sri Lanka: A Perfect Storm Threatening Civic Space

At least seven laws and draft bills enacted or circulated in Sri Lanka since 2023, combined with the rapid construction of a digital state, create a credible capacity to intimidate, incapacitate or criminalise dissent without declaring an emergency, warns researcher Sanjana Hattotuwa.

These instruments include the Online Safety Act, Anti-Corruption Act, Proceeds of Crime Act, the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA), the draft NGO Registration and Supervision Bill, and cybersecurity measures. Alongside them, the government is building a unique digital identity, national data exchange, upgraded government cloud, digital payments and a single public-services app. Human rights receive little attention in the accompanying AI and sovereign cloud strategies.

News Analysis;

The real danger lies not in any single clause but in the "interaction design" of these laws and digital systems working together. The Personal Data Protection Act remains only partly in force until January 2027, while the digital architecture hardens between 2026 and 2028 - before the next election. The Executive Presidency remains the terminus for key appointments and powers. Historical precedent (the use of voter lists against Tamil households in 1983) shows how digitisation removes earlier friction. Hattotuwa correctly argues that international funders, including the World Bank and UN agencies, should treat rights safeguards as conditions of disbursement rather than accompanying language. Weak safeguards and unequal enforcement make the risks especially severe for civil society and minority communities.

hitting our $1.2M ARR wasn't about going viral or huge ad spend.

it was boring, tiny site tweaks most people miss.

here are the 8 steps & prompts that boosted your traffic and conversions:

0. Understand the Full System

website optimization isn’t just about changing the design.

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

here’s what we review every month:

・pages gaining or losing search impressions
・pages gaining or losing traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI services
・pages with low click-through rates
・articles losing rankings
・high-traffic pages that don’t generate signups
・pages with speed issues
・traffic sources generating signups or purchases

we use NoimosAI agents to continuously identify keyword gaps and rewrite underperforming content.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to find the gap between you and your competitors:
“Every week, identify high-priority keywords that competitors rank for but we don’t, then create one new article idea.”

“Every month, compare the latest 28 days with the previous 28 days. Use search rankings, clicks, and traffic from AI services to identify the article with the highest improvement potential and create a rewrite plan.”

website optimization isn’t about launching a flashy redesign.

it’s about:

・building a system that measures results
・making your value easy to understand
・creating content around real customer problems
・improving continuously based on data

repeat this process, and your website stops being a static company brochure.

it becomes a system that consistently generates customers.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

मैं आपका ध्यान C.R. Park Post Office, New Delhi – 110019 में दिनांक 10.08.2026 को उत्पन्न गंभीर समस्या की ओर आकर्षित करना चाहता हूँ।

दिनांक 10 अगस्त 2026 को उक्त Post Office में कथित रूप से पूरे दिन Server/Online System Down रहा, जिसके कारण आम ग्राहकों को अपने आवश्यक डाक एवं अन्य सेवाओं से संबंधित कार्य कराने में भारी परेशानी का सामना करना पड़ा। लोगों का समय बर्बाद हुआ और कई ग्राहकों को बिना सेवा प्राप्त किए वापस लौटना पड़ा।

सबसे महत्वपूर्ण प्रश्न यह है कि यदि Department of Posts द्वारा सेवाओं के लिए शुल्क निर्धारित है और ग्राहक Cash में भुगतान करना चाहता है, तो क्या C.R. Park Post Office में Cash स्वीकार नहीं किया जा रहा है? यदि Cash Payment स्वीकार नहीं की जा रही है और केवल Online/Digital Payment के माध्यम से भुगतान करने के लिए कहा जा रहा है, तो कृपया स्पष्ट किया जाए कि:

1. क्या Department of Posts द्वारा ऐसा कोई आधिकारिक Circular/Order/Guideline जारी किया गया है जिसमें संबंधित सेवा के लिए Cash Payment स्वीकार न करने और केवल Online/Digital Payment लेने का निर्देश दिया गया हो?

2. यदि ऐसा कोई Circular/Order है, तो उसकी प्रति तथा Circular Number/Date सार्वजनिक की जाए।

3. क्या यह व्यवस्था सभी Post Offices में लागू है या केवल C.R. Park Post Office में ही ग्राहकों से Cash लेने से मना किया जा रहा है?

4. यदि Cash Payment स्वीकार करना विभागीय नियमों के अनुसार अनुमत है, तो C.R. Park Post Office में ग्राहकों से Cash लेने से मना करने का कारण क्या है?

5. दिनांक 10.08.2026 को पूरे दिन Server Down रहने का वास्तविक कारण क्या था? क्या यह Department का Central Server/System Issue था या स्थानीय Post Office का Internet/Hardware/Software संबंधी मामला था?

6. Server Down होने की स्थिति में ग्राहकों को वैकल्पिक व्यवस्था उपलब्ध कराने के लिए विभाग द्वारा क्या Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) निर्धारित है?

7. कृपया यह भी जांच की जाए कि Server/Online System बार-बार प्रभावित होने की स्थिति में ग्राहकों को अनावश्यक रूप से परेशान तो नहीं किया जा रहा है।

मैं यह भी स्पष्ट करना चाहता हूँ कि Department of Posts एक महत्वपूर्ण सार्वजनिक सेवा है। Digital Payment को बढ़ावा देना अलग विषय है, लेकिन यदि किसी सेवा में Cash Payment स्वीकार करने पर कोई प्रतिबंध लगाया गया है तो उसका स्पष्ट एवं लिखित विभागीय आधार होना चाहिए। केवल मौखिक रूप से ग्राहकों को यह कहना कि “Cash नहीं चलेगा, केवल Online Payment होगा” उचित नहीं होना चाहिए, जब तक इसके संबंध में सक्षम प्राधिकारी का स्पष्ट आदेश/निर्देश उपलब्ध न हो।

अतः निवेदन है कि इस मामले की उच्च स्तर पर जांच कराई जाए तथा C.R. Park Post Office के संबंधित अधिकारियों से स्पष्टीकरण लिया जाए।

साथ ही, कृपया मुझे निम्नलिखित जानकारी उपलब्ध कराने की कृपा करें:

- 10.08.2026 को Server Down रहने का कारण।
- Server Down की अवधि एवं संबंधित Technical Complaint/Ticket Number।
- Cash Payment स्वीकार न करने के संबंध में लागू Circular/Order/Guideline की प्रति।
- क्या यह व्यवस्था पूरे Delhi Postal Circle में लागू है या केवल C.R. Park Post Office में?
- भविष्य में ऐसी समस्या होने पर ग्राहकों के लिए उपलब्ध वैकल्पिक व्यवस्था।

The markings on the device indicated that they were brought in from Myanmar across the border.

Reports also indicated that a lot of these devices had been smuggled across the border. Internet signals were spilling over from Myanmar, and bad actors used them to bypass prolonged internet shutdowns during times of unrest.

Allowing internet infrastructure to be operated from outside the country makes it difficult for the government to effectively implement law-and-order measures in critical areas.

This has recently happened in many parts of the world, including Iran, according to news reports. This is what worries the Indian security agencies.

Satellite internet is not limited by boundaries. Agreed that the coverage can still be restricted or managed. Still, that control sits with a company operating from a foreign land.

On top of that, 100% foreign ownership is also spooking the authorities.

The technology is definitely useful and would help reduce the internet coverage gap FAST. But that would also open the door to misuse in places that India is most worried about, i.e., conflict zones, protests, and contested borders.

This is one of the sharpest test cases for satellite internet penetration in India, and it will be interesting to see how it plays out.

Amid heightened tensions and a heavy police presence in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan state in India, the local administration has begun demolishing a 44-year-old historic mosque. The operation was carried out on Sunday (June 7) to remove the historic Noorani Mosque, located in the Malviya Nagar area of Jaipur.

The four-story Noorani Mosque located in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, India, is being demolished by the authorities as part of a road-widening project. In connection with the operation, internet services across the city were suspended for 24 hours, and extensive security measures were put in place.

The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) claims that the mosque was constructed illegally on leased land. However, the mosque committee has rejected this allegation, stating that the land was legally purchased from a housing society in 1981 before the structure was built.

A large number of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area, drone surveillance is being conducted, and restrictive orders remain in effect throughout the operation. The mosque committee and several opposition lawmakers have criticized the move, alleging that proper procedures were not followed.

Authorities stated that the temporary internet shutdown was imposed to prevent the spread of rumors and misinformation and to maintain law and order during the demolition process. So far, the operation has remained peaceful, with no reports of violence or unrest.

Mobile internet was cut in parts of central Delhi as thousands of students marched on parliament. Here is what makes it worse than a routine shutdown. No suspension order has been published by anyone, which breaks India's own Supreme Court ruling and two of its own laws requiring published, written reasons. So the network goes dark exactly when people are protesting, and the government does not even follow its own process for doing it. India recorded 65 shutdowns in 2025, the most of any democracy on earth. A blackout during a protest, with no order and no reasons, is not security. It is a government switching off the witnesses.
#InternetFreedom #DigitalRights

5 AUGUST 2019 → 5 AUGUST 2026

SEVEN YEARS SINCE ARTICLE 370:
THE DAY KASHMIR CHANGED DIRECTION
Seven years ago, on 5 August 2019, Jammu and Kashmir underwent the most consequential constitutional reorganisation in its recent history.

The decision was immediately surrounded by anger, apprehension, predictions of permanent instability and declarations that Kashmir would never recover.

Seven years later, the argument must no longer be conducted through slogans.

It must be tested through outcomes.

> What disappeared?
> What emerged?
> What changed on the street?
> What reached the village?
> What entered the economy?
> And what still remains unfinished?

The honest answer is that 5 August was not a magic switch that transformed Kashmir overnight.
It was a structural reset.

It dismantled an exceptional political arrangement that had gradually become the protective vocabulary of dynastic entitlement, institutional ambiguity, separatist mobilisation and permanent emotional blackmail.

For decades, Kashmir was presented as a society that could only be administered through fear, negotiated with through shutdowns and represented through a handful of political families and separatist intermediaries.

The ordinary Kashmiri rarely controlled that narrative.
The gunman claimed to speak for him.
The separatist issued calendars in his name.
The politician traded his sentiment.
The propagandist exported his suffering.
And the shopkeeper, student, labourer and parent paid the bill.

THE STREET HAS CHANGED

In 2018, Jammu and Kashmir recorded 1,328 incidents of organised stone-pelting and 52 organised hartals.

By 2023, both figures had fallen to zero. The same remained true in official data reported through July 2024.

Terrorist-initiated incidents declined from 228 in 2018 to 46 in 2023.

This is not a cosmetic improvement.

It represents the collapse of an entire infrastructure of organised disruption.
There was a time when one WhatsApp message could empty a market.
One separatist calendar could shut an entire district.
One militant funeral could mobilise thousands.
One rumour could interrupt examinations, transport, business and public life.

Kashmir’s economy was being governed not by institutions, but by uncertainty.

Today, the culture of compulsory shutdown has largely disappeared.

The significance is not that Kashmiris have lost their political voice.

The significance is that coercion no longer decides whether a child attends school, whether a shop opens, whether a patient reaches hospital or whether a family can earn its daily income.

That is freedom too.

But honesty also requires a warning:

Terrorism has not vanished.

The Pahalgam attack of April 2025, in which 26 people were killed, demonstrated that Pakistan-backed terrorism retains the ability to inflict pain and disrupt progress.

Therefore, the achievement is not the complete elimination of the threat.

It is the reduction of terrorism’s social command over Kashmir.

The terrorist may still attempt an attack.

But he no longer automatically controls the street after it.

FROM BOYCOTT TO THE BALLOT

For years, elections in Kashmir were conducted under the shadow of boycott calls, threats, selective violence and claims that voting represented betrayal.

In 2024, Jammu and Kashmir voted in its first Assembly election in a decade.

The overall turnout was 63.88%.

The elections were completed peacefully, without major election-related violence and without repolling.

That figure represents more than electoral participation.

It marks a psychological transition.

The same population that was once instructed to remain behind closed doors stepped out to elect its representatives.

The ballot did not resolve every political disagreement.

It did something more important:

It restored the ordinary citizen to the centre of politics.

Democracy replaced the separatist veto.

Political parties were forced to seek votes instead of interpreting silence.

Even parties that opposed the 2019 decision participated fully in the constitutional process created after it.

That is the great irony of post-2019 Kashmir:

Those who continue to describe the new constitutional order as illegitimate now seek authority, office and political relevance through elections held under that very order.

The boycott has ended.

The bargaining has begun.

FROM EXCEPTION TO EQUAL RIGHTS

After the constitutional changes, 170 Central laws that had not previously applied in Jammu and Kashmir were extended to the region.

These included legal protections connected with education, transparency, minority rights, domestic violence, safeguards for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, forest rights and social justice.

For the first time, constitutional protections available elsewhere in India acquired uniform legal application in Jammu and Kashmir.

This did not automatically solve every injustice.

A law written in Delhi has value only when it is implemented honestly in Kupwara, Kishtwar, Poonch, Shopian and Srinagar.

But the principle changed fundamentally:

Rights would no longer depend on whether a regional political establishment considered their application convenient.

Article 370 had been marketed as a shield protecting every Kashmiri.

In practice, it also became a wall behind which several deprived communities remained politically invisible.

Its removal did not erase Kashmiri identity.

It removed the argument that equality before national law was somehow incompatible with that identity.

THE RAILWAY MAP HAS CHANGED

The transformation is now visible in steel, tunnels and bridges.

In June 2025, the 272-kilometre Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link was dedicated to the nation.

Built at an estimated cost of approximately ₹43,780 crore, the project includes:

— 36 tunnels covering around 119 kilometres
— 943 bridges
— The 359-metre-high Chenab Railway Bridge, the world’s highest railway arch bridge
— The Anji Bridge, India’s first cable-stayed railway bridge

Vande Bharat services now connect Jammu and Srinagar, reducing the journey to approximately three hours.

For generations, geography was treated as Kashmir’s permanent disadvantage.

Now engineering is beginning to convert that geography into connectivity.

An apple grower should not have to calculate his future according to a landslide.

A student should not feel nationally distant because a highway is closed.

A patient should not remain isolated by snow.

A business should not lose its market because the mountain has become impassable.

Rail connectivity is not merely infrastructure.

It is economic integration, strategic mobility and psychological proximity.

FROM AIRPORT CONGESTION TO EXPANSION

Srinagar Airport handled around 44.7 lakh passengers during FY 2024–25, despite its existing terminal being designed for a much smaller annual capacity.
In February 2026, a ₹1,677-crore expansion project was approved.
The plan is intended to increase annual passenger-handling capacity from 2.5 million to 10 million and raise peak-hour capacity from approximately 950 to 2,900 passengers.

That tells its own story.

The debate is no longer whether people will come to Kashmir.

The question is whether the infrastructure can accommodate how many are arriving.

TOURISM HAS RETURNED TO SCALE

Jammu and Kashmir recorded approximately 1.78 crore tourist arrivals in 2025, including around 36,000 foreign visitors.

These figures include different categories of visitors and pilgrimage traffic, and tourism remains vulnerable to security incidents.

Nevertheless, the direction is unmistakable.

Hotels that once calculated losses through curfew calendars now calculate occupancy.

Taxi drivers once trapped by shutdowns now depend on the length of the tourist season.

Houseboat owners, guides, artisans, restaurant workers, pony operators and small traders are again connected to a functioning visitor economy.

Earlier, instability was exported as Kashmir’s primary image.

Today, millions arrive to experience Kashmir directly.

That weakens propaganda more effectively than any press conference.

THE ECONOMY IS EXPANDING BUT MUST BECOME MORE INCLUSIVE

Jammu and Kashmir’s nominal economy is estimated at approximately ₹2.86 lakh crore in 2025–26.

Real GSDP is projected to grow by around 5.82%, while nominal growth is estimated at 8.89%.

Per-capita income is estimated at approximately ₹1.68 lakh.

The Economic Survey reports that over the preceding seven years, around 2,227 industrial units, involving investment of roughly ₹15,940 crore, became operational.

This reflects movement.

But investment announcements must not be confused with employment delivered.

A factory on a presentation slide does not provide a salary.

A memorandum of understanding is not an operational industry.

The next stage of transformation must therefore be judged by:

How many stable jobs are created?
How many local enterprises survive?
How much value is added to horticulture?
How many young people can build careers without leaving?
How many districts benefit beyond Srinagar and Jammu?

The old political economy survived by distributing government jobs, contracts and access through patronage.

The new economy must create opportunity beyond political recommendation.

Otherwise, development will remain visible in infrastructure but distant from households.

ENERGY: FROM POTENTIAL TO PRODUCTION

Major hydropower projects are now under construction, including:

— Pakal Dul: 1,000 MW
— Ratle: 850 MW
— Kiru: 624 MW
— Kwar: 540 MW

Together, these projects represent more than 3,000 MW of prospective generation capacity.

For a region with immense water resources but persistent power shortages, this is both opportunity and indictment.

Kashmir cannot indefinitely celebrate generation projects while households experience winter cuts.

The real success will come when hydropower is reflected not only in national capacity, but also in reliable local supply, fair benefits and visible economic returns.

THE MOST IMPORTANT TRANSFORMATION IS PSYCHOLOGICAL

The deepest change cannot be measured only in bridges, tourists or investment.

It lies in what Kashmir’s new generation now considers normal.
A generation once trained to recognize protest calendars is now discussing start-ups, examinations, sport, cinema, tourism, technology and entrepreneurship.
The romantic vocabulary of militancy has weakened.
The social prestige attached to street confrontation has declined.
Parents increasingly recognize that political entrepreneurs who glorified sacrifice rarely sacrificed their own children.

The separatist elite promised dignity through disorder.

But ordinary Kashmiris discovered that disorder always protects the powerful and punishes the poor.

The wealthy sent their children outside.

The shopkeeper remained behind a locked shutter.

The leader delivered speeches.

The labourer lost his wage.
The propagandist gained engagement.
The Kashmiri family received a funeral.
That business model has been disrupted.

BUT TRANSFORMATION IS NOT COMPLETION

A serious defence of 5 August must not become a denial of Kashmir’s unresolved problems.

Statehood remains pending.

Unemployment continues to frustrate young people.

Drug addiction has become a grave social emergency.

Power shortages remain unacceptable.

Recruitment processes require greater transparency.

Local businesses need protection against unequal competition.

Governance must become more accountable.

Terror networks continue to search for vulnerabilities.

And democratic institutions must be strengthened—not managed from a distance.

Peace cannot merely mean the absence of stones.

It must mean the presence of justice, opportunity, representation and responsive government.

Security created the space.

Politics and governance must now fill it.

SEVEN YEARS LATER

Before 2019, Kashmir was too often measured through:

=> Shutdown days.
=> Stone-pelting incidents.
=> Militant funerals.
=> Internet suspensions.
=> Boycott percentages.
=> Civilian casualties.
=> And economic losses.

Today, the conversation increasingly revolves around:

=> Voter turnout.
=> Tourist arrivals.
=> Rail connectivity.
=> Airport capacity.
=> Industrial units.
=> Investment.
=> Infrastructure.
=> And opportunity.

That is the transformation.

Not perfection.

Not the end of every conflict.

Not the disappearance of every grievance.

But a decisive change in direction.

5 August did not take Kashmir away from its identity.

It took away the monopoly of those who claimed that Kashmir’s identity could survive only through isolation, exceptionalism and endless instability.

Seven years later, the old ecosystem still mourns the loss of its political currency.

But Kashmir is no longer obliged to mourn with it.

The Valley has moved from enforced silence to democratic participation.

From shutdown calendars to train timetables.

From stone-pelting statistics to tourism figures.

From emotional exploitation to economic aspiration.

From a conflict managed by intermediaries to a future increasingly claimed by ordinary people.

5 August 2019 was not the day Kashmir lost its future.

It was the day those who had monopolized Kashmir’s future began losing control over it.

The transformation is visible.

The responsibility now is to deepen it, democratize it and ensure that its benefits reach every household.

Because the final measure of a new Kashmir will not be how loudly governments celebrate the change.

It will be how fully ordinary Kashmiris experience it.
#TransformingKashmir #Kashmir

Dimagi Naxal is trending.
Modi dropped two words.

And suddenly,
some people filed self-nominations.

Nobody named them.
Nobody pointed at them.

Yet a few jumped up:
“Yes. Proud to be Dimagi Naxal.”

Beautifully foolish.

The people of India are now confused.

“Sir… was that an accusation?”
“Or a confession?”

Jokes apart, the subject is serious.

Armed Naxalism can be hunted.
Ideological Naxalism is hidden .

Because they wear no uniform.

They may carry no gun.
They may sit beside you.

At home.
At work.
In a university.
Inside an institution.
Even inside politics.

But here is the warning.

Criticism is NOT Naxalism.
Opposing Modi is not Naxalism.
Opposing Government is not Naxalism.
Protesting is not Naxalism.
Being Left-wing is not Naxalism.
Democracy needs disagreement.

So what should worry us?

Watch the conduct.
Not the costume.

The conversation changes first.

Violence becomes “resistance.”
Killings become “revolution.”
Democracy becomes “useless.”
The Constitution becomes “bourgeois.”
Armed struggle becomes “necessary.”

Then comes romanticisation.

A massacre gets an excuse.
A slain jawan gets a lecture.
A banned outfit gets sympathy.

Sometimes the clues are louder.

Listen to the slogans.

“Afzal, hum sharminda hain…”
“Kashmir ki azaadi tak…”
“Bharat ki barbadi tak…”
“Free Umar Khalid.”

These are serious red flags for any Intelligence officer.
And should be for every citizen too.

Then comes recruitment.

“Meet these people.”
“Don't mention this outside.”
“You can contribute more.”

Then comes the network.

Money moves strangely.
Meetings become secretive.
Contacts become organised.

Logistics appear.
Couriers appear.
Support starts getting practical.

And social media tells stories too.

Not one angry post.
Not one stupid comment.
Look for a pattern.

Glorifying armed revolution.
Justifying political murder.

Recruiting for violent causes.
Defending banned formations.

Fundraising for linked networks.
Turning every atrocity into theory.

That is where ideology starts becoming infrastructure.

A dissenter asks questions.
An extremist normalises violence.

A democrat wants reform.
An insurgent wants collapse.

So don't hunt people.
Observe behaviour.

Don't profile faces.
Follow patterns.

Don't call every critic a Naxal.
That only helps the real ones hide.

The dangerous naxal may never shout.
May never carry a weapon.
May never enter a jungle.

Sometimes, the gun is kilometres away.

But the justification,
money,
recruitment,
and narrative
may be sitting in an air-conditioned room.

That is the real challenge.

And perhaps the funniest part?

Modi merely said:
“Identify them.”

Some people apparently replied:
“Attendance, sir!”

The Global Geoengineering Network: Corporations, Governments, and Hidden Agendas

This is a well-documented global industry driven by private capital, government agencies, and multinational corporations. Here are the key players, technologies, and evidence behind this global geoengineering movement.

I. Private Companies: Profit-Driven Pioneers of Geoengineering

These companies are not merely "studying" the weather; they are actively deploying weather-modification measures and profiting from them.

1. Rainmaker (USA)

▪️Founder and CEO: Augustus Doricko (26), a UC Berkeley dropout.
▪️ Operations: Uses drones for cloud seeding to increase rainfall and snowfall in drought-stricken regions.
▪️Scale: Has raised $6.3 million in funding and operates one of the largest cloud-seeding projects in U.S. history. Doricko claims his technology represents "the biggest step in water infrastructure since the invention of the aqueduct."
🔸 Evidence:
  ▪️NewsNation report: https://t.co/ceMQLemnUV
  ▪️Podcast interview: https://t.co/vsYmF0hh9u

2. Stardust Solutions (Israel-USA)

▪️Operations: Solar Radiation Management (SRM) spraying millions of tons of reflective particles into the stratosphere to block sunlight and cool the Earth.
▪️Funding: Has raised $75 million since 2023. Investors are betting that governments will eventually foot the bill for this service.  
▪️Plan: Outdoor experiments were initially scheduled to begin in April 2026. The composition of the particles used to be a "closely guarded secret."
🔸 Evidence:
  ▪️ The Times of Israel: https://t.co/8TjOG4hXpi
  ▪️ Politico: https://t.co/dYfdA7SF2L

3. Make Sunsets (USA)

Operations: Releases sulfur dioxide (SO₂) into the stratosphere via high-altitude balloons to simulate the cooling effect of volcanic eruptions.
▪️Business Model: Sells "Cooling Credits."
▪️Scale: Since February 2023, it has delivered over 140 kilograms of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere using more than 160 balloons.
▪️ Controversy: Mexico has banned related experiments due to the company's activities. Scientists have criticized the initiative as "unverified by anyone."
🔸 Evidence:
  ▪️ SRM360: https://t.co/fMC61evKPL
  · Chesapeake Climate Action Network: https://t.co/K2l07AAiX8

4. Other Players

▪️Supercool Earth: Uses proteins produced by engineered microorganisms for cloud seeding.
▪️Skyward #Wildfire: Uses cloud seeding to prevent lightning strikes and thereby reduce wildfires.
▪️Silver Lining: Another company focused on solar radiation management.

II. Governments: National-level weather modification programs

According to data from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), at least 50 countries are conducting weather modification experiments.  

Country | Project Scale/Status | Remarks
🇨🇳 China | World's largest weather modification program | National-level strategy; used to increase precipitation, suppress hail, etc.
🇺🇸 USA | Large-scale cloud seeding projects | Ongoing weather modification projects across 11 western states.
🇦🇪 UAE | Active cloud seeding program | Utilizes drones and new technologies.
🇮🇳 India | Experimental cloud seeding | Used to alleviate drought.
🇷🇺 Russia | Experimental cloud seeding | Includes cloud seeding to ensure clear skies for events in Moscow.
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia | Experimental cloud seeding | Used to increase precipitation.
🇦🇺 Australia | Government-supported projects | Long-term projects in Tasmania and other regions.
🇫🇷 France | Experimental cloud seeding | 
🇲🇦 Morocco | National-level program since 1985 | "Al-Ghait" project.
🇲🇱 Mali | National-level cloud seeding | 
🇳🇪 Niger | National-level cloud seeding | 

🔸Evidence:
  ▪️WION News: https://t.co/UBzB3VvPGF
  ▪️ CNBC: https://t.co/B734TBDBQI

III. Key Figures and Funders

▪️Bill Gates: Directly funded Harvard University's Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx). He has publicly stated: "Yes, I have been a funder of understanding geoengineering." He supports plans to spray millions of tons of chalk (calcium carbonate) into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight.
▪️Augustus Doricko: Founder of Rainmaker; Thiel Fellow; age 26.
▪️Luke Iseman: Co-founder of Make Sunsets.
▪️Janos Pasztor: Former UN climate official; serves as an advisor to Stardust Solutions.

IV. Technology: From Silver Iodide to Graphene Oxide

Weather modification technology is shifting from traditional methods to nanomaterials.  Traditional methods: Cloud seeding using silver iodide or dry ice.

Novel nanomaterials: A US patent (US 2022/0002159 A1) describes a 3D reduced graphene oxide/silica nanoparticle composite (PrGO-SN) for cloud seeding. This material can trigger ice nucleation at temperatures as high as -8°C. Voices on social media have already raised alarms: "They are patenting the sky and pumping graphene oxide into our clouds."

  ▪️Full patent text: https://t.co/ecY4Z8nKGp

V. Facts about HAARP

HAARP (High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program) is frequently linked to weather weaponry. However:

▪️HAARP’s radio waves cannot interact with the troposphere or stratosphere, where weather is generated.
▪️HAARP Director Jessica Matthews has stated that the facility "cannot create or amplify weather events in any way."
▪️Scientists have repeatedly pointed out that there is no known mechanism by which HAARP could create or intensify weather events.

HAARP does not control the weather. But private companies and governments are doing so.

Weather modification is no longer science fiction. It is a multi-billion-dollar industry operating on a global scale:

▪️Rainmaker is deploying drones in the western US to increase precipitation via cloud seeding.
▪️Stardust Solutions is preparing to spray particles into the stratosphere to block sunlight.
▪️Make Sunsets is already releasing sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere.

And the world is allowing it to happen.

text:
LIES! LIES! LIES! @himantabiswa MISLEADS ASSAM AND CONTEMPTS THE COURT IN HIS INTERPRETATION OF KAZIRANGA JUDGEMENT

The people of Assam are being systematically misled. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma is presenting a carefully constructed narrative that the proposal to shrink the Eco-Sensitive Zone around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve from the default 10 km to a mere 1 km (or 1–3 km) is a routine, court-mandated exercise that will harm neither wildlife nor the ecological integrity of this UNESCO World Heritage Site. This claim is false. It is a deliberate distortion of the law, the record of the Gauhati High Court, and the consistent directions of the Supreme Court of India. The real objective is to create legal space for mining and commercial activity in the fragile southern landscape of Kaziranga—activity that has already been repeatedly restrained by the highest court of the land.

What follows is a step-by-step, legally grounded account of the true position:

1. The Foundation: How Kaziranga Became a Protected Area

Kaziranga’s protection is not a recent administrative convenience. It began in the colonial era and was progressively strengthened by independent India’s wildlife law.

In 1905 the area was proposed as a Reserve Forest. It was notified as a Reserved Forest in 1908 and upgraded to a Game Sanctuary in 1916. In 1950 it became a Wildlife Sanctuary. On 11 February 1974, vide Notification No. FOR/WL/722/68 issued under Section 8(1)(b) of the Assam National Park Act, 1968, the Governor of Assam declared an area of approximately 429.93 sq km a National Park with effect from 1 January 1974. The notification contains a precise boundary description by rivers, bearings and distances.

Subsequent additions under Section 35 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 expanded the Park. On 3 August 2007, Notification No. FRW-6/2007/23 under Section 38V declared the larger landscape a Tiger Reserve: core area 48,203.85 ha (including the original National Park and several additions) and buffer 54,835.55 ha (including further additions, reserved forests and the Laokhowa and Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuaries), totalling approximately 1,030 sq km.

These notifications fix the legal boundary of the protected area. Any Eco-Sensitive Zone is measured outward from that boundary. The buffer of the Tiger Reserve is an internal management zone; it is not a substitute for the regulatory Eco-Sensitive Zone under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Supreme Court directions.

2. The Supreme Court’s ESZ Framework

The Supreme Court has repeatedly addressed Eco-Sensitive Zones in the T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad proceedings (W.P. (C) No. 202 of 1995).

On 3 June 2022 the Court directed that every national park and wildlife sanctuary must have a minimum 1 km ESZ measured from its demarcated boundary. Where a wider zone was already prescribed by law or a wider proposal was awaiting final decision, the wider margin would prevail. Crucially, where no State or Union Territory proposal had been submitted, the 10 km buffer zone indicated in the 2006 Goa Foundation order and the 2011 Guidelines would operate, and the entire set of ESZ restrictions would apply until a final decision was taken. Mining inside national parks and wildlife sanctuaries was prohibited.

On 26 April 2023 the Court modified the mandatory 1 km direction. It held that a uniform 1 km zone was not feasible in every case and that the direction would not apply where a draft or final notification had already been issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change or where proposals had been received by the Ministry. The Court retained the absolute prohibition on mining within the protected area and within 1 km of its boundary. The 10 km default direction for areas where no proposal had been submitted remained in force.

In short, the Supreme Court never authorised States to unilaterally shrink an existing protective default. It required a formal, site-specific proposal, central scrutiny, and a final notification. Until that process is completed, the 10 km default continues.

3. The Gauhati High Court Record: What the Court Actually Said

Order dated 12 March 2026 (Justice Manish Choudhury) in Jiten Engjai v. Union of India (WP(C)/6479/2025)
This is the order repeatedly invoked by the Chief Minister. The petition challenged the suspension of a stone quarry in the Parkup Pahar Range on the ground that it fell within the default Eco-Sensitive Zone of Kaziranga.

The Court examined the Supreme Court orders of 3 June 2022 and 26 April 2023 in detail. On a specific query, the Standing Counsel for the Environment and Forest Department of Assam submitted that as on 12 March 2026 there was neither any final notification nor any draft proposal on the Eco-Sensitive Zone of Kaziranga National Park from the State Government that had been submitted to the Central Government. The Court therefore held that the 10 km Eco-Sensitive Zone remained operative. Paragraph 61 of the 26 April 2023 order (the exemption for already-notified or proposed ESZs) was held inapplicable.

The Court also recalled the Supreme Court’s 12 April 2019 order restraining all mining and related activities along the southern boundary of Kaziranga and in the entire catchment of rivers, streams and rivulets originating in the Karbi Anglong hills and flowing into the Park, as well as the prohibition on new construction on private lands forming part of the nine identified animal corridors.

Order dated 11 August 2026 (Justice Devashis Baruah) in the batch of connected petitions

This later order deals with the continued suspension of several stone quarries following directions issued by the Central Empowered Committee. The Court noted the sequence of events, including the CEC’s communication of 30 May 2025, and observed that the powers conferred on the CEC under the 5 September 2023 notification appear limited to monitoring and making recommendations rather than issuing binding directions. The Court sought clarification from the Government of India on the scope of the CEC’s authority and listed the matters for further hearing on 3 September 2026. It did not disturb the factual finding of 12 March 2026 that no ESZ proposal for Kaziranga had been submitted and that the 10 km default therefore continued to operate.

4. What Activities Are Prohibited and Permitted in an Eco-Sensitive Zone

Under the 2011 Guidelines and the Supreme Court’s directions:
Prohibited activities include commercial mining, stone quarrying, and related industrial operations; setting up of new major hydro-electric projects; discharge of untreated effluents; and establishment of polluting industries.

Regulated activities include construction (subject to height and density restrictions), tourism facilities, and certain agricultural or forest-related activities, all requiring prior approval.

Permitted activities are limited to those that do not adversely affect the ecology—essentially traditional habitation and certain eco-development works.

Even if a narrower site-specific ESZ is eventually notified, mining remains absolutely prohibited within 1 km of the protected-area boundary. The Supreme Court has been consistent on this point. Any attempt to portray a reduction of the buffer as authorising mining closer to Kaziranga is legally false.

5. The Pattern of Illegal Mining and the Name of RS Gandhi

The southern landscape of Kaziranga has long been plagued by illegal stone and sand mining. The Supreme Court’s 12 April 2019 order was itself based on reports of such activity. The Central Empowered Committee has repeatedly recorded that mining continued and even intensified despite the ban. In 2025 the CEC reported fresh permissions granted by the Karbi Anglong Autonomous Council in violation of the Supreme Court’s directions and without the required approvals under the Forest (Conservation) Act.

Ranbir Singh Gandhi (RS Gandhi) of Hills Trade Agencies has been named in petitions before the Supreme Court and in public complaints as a prominent operator of stone quarries in Assam, including in areas under scrutiny near the Kaziranga landscape (Jagiroad, Panimara and related sites). Courts and the CEC have taken cognisance of these allegations. The pattern is clear: despite judicial restraints, commercial mining interests continue to press against the southern boundary of the Park. What is his relation to @Pijush_hazarika 

6. Why Protection Is More Urgent Than Ever: Rare Earth Elements

The Geological Survey of India has identified significant Rare Earth Element resources in the Jashora Ultramafic Alkaline Complex and the Samchampi-Samteran belt in Karbi Anglong. It is precisely the landscape that forms the southern refuge for Kaziranga’s wildlife during floods. Resource estimates of the order of 28.64 million tonnes have been reported at G3 level, with further exploration under way. These critical minerals are of strategic national importance. Their presence only heightens the need for rigorous ecological safeguards. 

Any weakening of the buffer around Kaziranga risks opening the door to mining pressures that could permanently damage the hydrology, wildlife corridors and floodplain ecology of one of the world’s most important protected areas.

7. The Political Deception

Himanta Biswa Sarma claims that a 10 km zone would “finish” towns such as Bokakhat, Kaliabor and Jakhalabandha and even force the closure of the Numaligarh Refinery. This is scare-mongering. The 10 km default has operated for years without extinguishing these settlements. The Supreme Court itself recognised in 2023 that day-to-day activities of citizens should not be unduly hampered, while simultaneously insisting that mining near protected areas remains forbidden.

The Chief Minister’s insistence that the State is merely following Supreme Court directions ignores the High Court’s own record: as of March 2026 the State had submitted no proposal at all. The sudden urgency to notify a narrow zone, while stone quarries remain under active judicial scrutiny and while rare-earth exploration intensifies in the same hills, reveals the real priority—facilitating commercial extraction under the cover of a “scientific” notification.

Kaziranga is not merely a tourist destination or a political talking point. It is the last major stronghold of the one-horned rhinoceros, a critical tiger habitat, and an irreplaceable floodplain ecosystem. Animals do not recognise administrative lines drawn on maps; during the annual floods they move into the Karbi Anglong foothills. A 1 km buffer offers them no meaningful refuge once mining, crushers and industrial activity occupy the adjoining landscape.

The @INCAssam  demands that the State Government immediately place before the public and the courts the complete scientific basis, if any, for the proposed 1 km zone; that all mining and related activities in the southern catchment remain strictly restrained in accordance with the Supreme Court’s 2019 and subsequent directions; and that the ecological integrity of Kaziranga not be sacrificed for short-term commercial gain. The people of Assam deserve the truth, not carefully packaged misrepresentation.

What started as a challenge to demolition proceedings against a G+1 building erected without sanction in Chennai quickly revealed a deeper pattern. The Court observed that such a construction could not have come up unnoticed. It spoke of collusion and connivance of municipal authorities and an “alarming state of affairs.”

Instead of confining itself to one petitioner, the Division Bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan converted the matter into a continuing supervisory jurisdiction over urban governance across the country. Municipal corporations of state capitals were impleaded. Chief Secretaries of every State and Union Territory were brought on record. An Amicus Curiae was appointed as nodal officer for citizen complaints. Affidavits were demanded, personal appearances ordered, and costs enhanced for non-compliance.
